title: India Just Replaced Its Biggest Rural Jobs Programme. Not Everyone Thinks the Replacement Is an Upgrade.
excerpt: MGNREGA is dead. The new VB-G RAM G scheme promises 125 days of work — but states, including BJP ones, say the funding model could bankrupt them.
body:
India's most far-reaching rural welfare programme just changed hands. On July 1, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act — MGNREGA, the 21-year-old law that promised 100 days of paid manual work to every rural household — was formally repealed and replaced by the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), or VB-G RAM G.

The new law, passed by Parliament in December 2025 and notified for nationwide implementation on May 11, raises the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days per financial year. It also introduces weekly wage disbursement instead of the old fortnightly cycle, a move designed to improve cash flow for some of India's poorest families.

But the transition is far from a simple upgrade. The Centre has fundamentally redrawn how the programme is funded, governed and delivered — and the changes have drawn pushback from states across party lines, including several governed by the BJP itself.

## The money question

Under MGNREGA, the central government bore the entire wage cost. States paid only for materials, roughly 10 per cent of the total outlay. VB-G RAM G shifts to a 60:40 cost-sharing model between the Centre and states — a change that could dramatically increase the financial burden on state treasuries.

RTI records obtained by the National Campaign for People's Right to Information reveal the scale of the impact. Bihar's liability would balloon from ₹4,477 crore under the old model to an estimated ₹15,939 crore under the new one. Madhya Pradesh's share would jump from ₹4,168 crore to ₹20,037 crore. Jharkhand's would more than quintuple, from ₹1,804 crore to ₹9,293 crore.

Uttarakhand, which currently receives central funds under a more generous 90:10 ratio owing to its difficult terrain, has urged the Centre to continue bearing the full wage cost. Sikkim has raised similar concerns.

## The 60-day blackout

Perhaps the most contentious provision is a 60-day "blackout period" during peak agricultural seasons, when no employment will be offered under the scheme. The government says this ensures adequate farm-labour availability during harvest and sowing periods. Critics argue it strips rural workers of their bargaining power precisely when they need it most, and could trigger distress migration to cities during the pause.

Four state governments have formally opposed the blackout provision, according to RTI disclosures shared by the Rural Development Ministry across 13 states.

## Dropping the name

The rebranding has not gone unnoticed. Congress leader Jairam Ramesh accused the Modi government of being "vengeful and petty" for removing Mahatma Gandhi's name from the programme, saying the repeal was "bulldozed through Parliament" without adequate consultation with the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Rural Development or state governments.

"MGNREGA guaranteed a right to work derived from the Constitution," Ramesh said. "VB-G RAM G will guarantee only centralisation and further financial stress on states."

## What the government says

Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has defended the overhaul, pointing to what he called "massive misuse of funds" and "several discrepancies" under MGNREGA. The Centre has allocated ₹95,692 crore to states for the programme and deputed officials to ensure a smooth transition.

The government has also emphasised continuity: existing MGNREGA job cards remain valid until new "Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards" are issued, ongoing projects will be carried forward, and workers will not be denied employment due to pending e-KYC verification.

The new law shifts planning from a demand-driven model to what the government calls "normative allocation," integrating rural employment with broader infrastructure goals through "Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans." Works will focus on four thematic areas: water security, core rural infrastructure, livelihood-related infrastructure and extreme-weather mitigation.

## Why NRIs should care

For the millions of diaspora Indians who send money home to families in rural India, the transition carries real stakes. Remittances often supplement the meagre wages that MGNREGA provided — and any disruption to the employment guarantee, particularly during the 60-day blackout window, could increase financial pressure on families that depend on both income streams. The cost-sharing shift also raises questions about whether fiscally weaker states will be able to sustain the higher employment guarantee without central support — precisely the states where NRI families are most likely to depend on the programme as a safety net.
